“The concept of territory is a completely Western idea."

Incorrect. Not all First Nations /and Inuit are the same nor is the territory of their current title and claims.

The plains, prarie, and boreal had more nomadic cultures to follow the game and seasons.

Contrast that to the Pacific coast where more favourable climates and local sustance/aquaculture permit year round and static villages. That returned territorial tribal and nation land territory with distinction between adversaries.

A recent Crown court ruling had the Nuchatlaht's claim applying first contact European impressions:

Captain James Cook to bolster their case. He wrote: "King George's Sound was the appellation given by the Commodore to this inlet, on our first arrival; but he was afterwards informed that the natives called it Nootka."

Quoted in court were Cook's writing about how the indigenous people he met on Nootka had "such high notions of everything the country produced being their exclusive property".

"The very wood and water we took on board they at first wanted us to pay for, and we had certainly done it, had I been upon the spot when the demands were made."

I absolutely agree. Whenever I see a ‘land acknowledgment’, I have to ask - are you paying rent to the descendants of the people who once lived there? If not, then you should just be quiet. Your virtue signaling is just insulting.

I saw a very annoying one recently on a building not far from my house, and it wasn’t just because they weren’t paying rent to the descendants of the local band of Ohlone - it’s because virtually the entire western half of San Francisco is built on sand dunes; in some areas 100+ feet high dunes that would shift overnight with the winds, burying anything in their way. Not to mention the cold, saturating fog much of the year! Don’t tell me the natives lived there when the eastern part of the peninsula was a paradise of meadows, streams, wetlands, forests and moderate weather. For the most part, the dunes were virtually unlivable until steam shovels and mule teams showed up to flatten them.

Anyway, anyone who actually IS paying rent to the original owners of the land doesn’t need to signal their virtue. In fact, if one actually is doing the right thing, piously proclaiming it kind of cancels out the good deed.

Native Americans got run over no doubt about it but I feel most land acknowledgment are just insincere performance art. How many think that whoever is writing the acknowledgment really cares? My guess is they are just following the political and cultural trade winds.

Worse yet are the acknowledgments that are just plain wrong. A classic example is the new (and very beautiful) Calder Museum in downtown Philadelphia. Their brochure has a land acknowledgment stating that the museum is on " unceded land". This factually incorrect. In 1682 William Penn entered into a voluntary treaty with the Lenape to live on the land that is now Philadelphia and included land on which the Calder Museum sits. By all accounts Penn was respected by the Lenape and he respected them. After his death things feel apart as a result of Penn's sons shady Walking Purchase.

In the meantime, land acknowledgment just begins the conversation.

The Wappinger Nation

comments.name: Daniel
comments.body: As a long-time traveler (pre-toddler), I find Ms. Ober's tone and assumptions so completely disconnected from reality that they undermine the general thrust of the article. The U.S. State Departments advisories are by all accounts relatively meaningless. To take those at face value is akin to saying "there's a 75% chance of rain." In reality, risks faced are far more nuanced than those advisories would suggest. A high murder rate in a state in Mexico, for example, doesn't mean that at any given moment and any given place your risk of being killed is increased. Cartels are more strategic in their activities, and American tourists are fairly low on the priority list of cartel targets. As another example (I wasn't tapped into the State Dept's warnings for this): many years ago I visited Galle, Sri Lanka, shortly after an attempted LTTE attack on the Sri Lankan navy. The attack was repelled, and that was that, but the tourists disappeared immediately. I was the only one in town. But the risk of being blown up by an LTTE sea attack, already essentially nil, was exactly zero, yet people still stayed away. Peoples' senses of risk are extremely warped. The State Department takes statistics and applies them meaninglessly to vast regions. This isn't to say everywhere is a paradise, and you should certainly plan ahead, but the reliance on State Department statistics as an indicator of overall risk is not based on real-world experience.

They still have the prevention mindset and have not changed to the adaptation mind set which is where the world regrettably finds itself now. 
There were emergency sirens day and night because of people in health emergencies. It reminded me of the worst days of Covid. A conservative number of the people who died from heat in Europe so far this summer is around 10,000 people and there is more analysis and heatwaves to come. 
They need AC available in many more pubic places -- especially on all metros and busses and trains. They need to protect the most vulnerable -- the elderly, sick, pregnant, and very young. They should replace the zinc roofs which makes the houses hot boxes that retain heat. The government should make it easier for people to air condition their homes if they want it.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
This piece brings back memories.  I’m old enough to remember the slogan — “Better Dead Than Red” — a Cold War artifact that still snaps into my head the moment one sees rhetoric about communism or socialism being used as a political cudgel. It captured the 1950s mood of existential fear, the sense that communism wasn’t just a rival ideology but an apocalyptic threat to American identity.  It’s striking that the old emotional trigger is being repurposed to frame frames political opponents — including groups like the Democratic Socialists of America — not as ideological rivals but as dangerous extremists. That’s a familiar pattern: Cold War rhetoric often blurred the line between policy disagreement and civilizational threat, and politicians found it to be a powerful mobilizing tool.  

You won't hear Better Dead Than Red today because Red no longer refers to communists but rather republicans and republican states.

comments.name: Wide Awake
comments.body: The strength of the Red Scare in the 1950s bore an inverse relation to the strength of the Communist movement in the United States.  The Communist Party had been driven out of the labor movement, its former stronghold, and held not a single elected position in the US. The fear of Communist infiltration grew to pathological levels precisely because so few Americans had ever encountered a real Communist.  Today, most Americans know who Zohran Mamdani is, know who AOC is.  They may disagree with them -- but they are not a phantom menace.  We'll see what happens, but I think that the presence of real socialists in positions of power (not Communists) will limit the effectiveness of Trump's Red Scare.

What one thinks about a party or political movement may be twisted and turned on its head leaving followers demoralized, and perhaps impoverished, imprisoned or possibly executed by the very same people that they helped bring to power. After seventy years of enduring brutal political regimes, Russians finally escaped their own he’ll only to have forgotten almost a century of lessons with a decade or so. comments.name: Invictus
comments.body:
As a psychologist, the good doctor should know that living next to a building that emits a constant whirring noise at decibel levels that interfere with sleep can have a detrimental effect on mental as well as physical health.

According to a recent article in the NYT, data centers emit sound waves that fall beneath the threshold of human hearing. Instead of hearing them, people feel them as pressure fluctuations. Some people that live near data centers report sleeplessness, anxiety, and internal ear pressure.  This says nothing of the vibrations that people feel from these behemoths. 
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/us/data-centers-noise-pollution.html

And when the good doctor speaks of water consumption, perhaps instead of making specious arguments about golf courses and lawns, he should go out west and talk to the ranchers there who are opposed to a massive data centers in their communities. Those ranchers ask the operative question: when the choice has to be made between water for a data center and water for the rest of us, who do you think will win that battle? (Hint: not us)

People across the country know the answer to that question and they are taking action. This isn't just a matter of NIMBY-ism; it's a matter of survival.  We don't need A.I., but we all need water.

comments.body:
I get how NIMBY makes it more likely that data centers will be pushed into less organized and affluent communities, but that doesn’t make “Sure, stick it IMBY” the solution. It means better regulation at the state and federal level to better manage the use of our resources. 

The problem I, and many others, have is that AI and the data centers they require ARE being foisted on us. They are required for iphone updates. Google just decided we all get AI whenever we search. And, yes, they are taking all of our data and using it however they want. No one has time to read all the EULAs but I bet Claude can tell you there are plenty of ways it can mine your data, if it was going to be honest, which it is not designed to be, and doesn’t KNOW how to be. 

So local protests are the ONLY way we can push back. They should be a sign that obscures rules, lack of regulation, no accountability, and indulgent tax laws are the problem - not we are all luddites who just don’t know how to use AI properly.

It was hot and greasy in the kitchen but that was better than waiting on customers who asked dumb questions ("How many pieces are in the six-piece dinner?") or tried to flirt with me, a 16-year-old kid.

The busiest day of the year? Mother's Day, of course. We came in early and filled the holding ovens with product but keeping up with the demand was not possible. I was sent to the busiest KFC to pack orders--my strong suit. I was not bored. 

And that concludes my stroll down memory lane.

No, it's not OK to hate. Hatred is corrosive to the character of the hater, and raises the potential for violence against the hated. 

Oh, you say, relax, it's just a figure of speech. "Summer" is not harmed by casual hatred. 

No, summer is not harmed. Society is harmed. 

Words have power. If you grow up saying that you hate things like the Yankees or Chevy trucks, that makes it much easier to hate Chevy truck drivers or Yankee fans--nameless and faceless groups. It's a small step from there to hating nationalities, which are NOT nameless and faceless people, and then of course your hatred easily extends to INDIVIDUALS in those groups. 

Hatred has been normalized in American discourse. As a legitimate human emotion, hatred cannot be dismissed. But hatred makes it easy to rationalize violence against the hated. Look at Israel and Palestine. Due to the harm it causes (to the hater AND the hated) and the infectious nature of hatred, encouraging or tolerating expressions of it diminishes society. 

There are plenty of elegant ways to express disapproval. Some of them are even uplifting. Hate all you want, but society doesn't benefit from your breezy and casual expressions of it.

comments.name: Andy
comments.body:
Speaking as a parent, one-time Boy Scout, and someone who spent years in the outdoor industry, I highly, highly recommend scouting for girls. It really is the only organization at that age-level that teaches the early skills that make lifelong outdoor pursuits safe and fun. 

Tying knots, planning meals, orienteering, and first aid are all things I learned at weekly meetings in a church basement. The weekend trips provided opportunities to apply these skills.This foundation provided a baseline knowledge for countless different adventures as a young adult. I wouldn’t have learned them anywhere else.

I remember comparing learning experiences with women who had to learn all this stuff without the help of Scouts. The alternatives almost universally fell into two categories: NOLS and working for Outward Bound. Both have their unique advantages but neither one is a 1:1 replacement for the ease and access of Scouting. The organization already exists. There’s no reason to reinvent the wheel. We just need to adapt it to serve two groups instead of one.

That said, I think the author slightly misreads the argument in favor of keeping Troops single gender. Scouting is as much about providing kids with a safe space to outgrow the awkwardness of puberty without the self-consciousness of gender awareness. Scouting contained an abundance of humiliating moments. Keeping it single gender minimizes the social impact of these growing pains.

We also did lots of community service, sang a lot of sings, and learned that Girl Scouts make the world a better place. And earn f the Girl Scout Gold Award is every bit as impressive as an achievement as earning the Boy Scout Eagle Award — and actually tougher because Girl Scouts require that their projects be sustainable . Let’s be clear: Boy Scouts started admitting girls as their numbers (and revenue) declined amid scandal — to poach members (and volunteers and money) from Girl Scouts.  While many girls are happy to be included, it’s a sad fact that that doesn’t go the other way in a society that teaches boys doing “girl stuff” is nothing but shameful.

We did hiking and many camping trips, including one winter camp where we pitched tents in the snow and learned how to stay warm in challenging weather (clean, dry socks was one tip!). I was a counselor for a day camp for young girls scouts and we stayed overnights in our tents to be ready for the crew everyday.  It was lovely freedom and hard work because we cleaned the whole camp every evening.  After 10 years and meeting all the requirements, I was awarded the “First Class” scout award which was as close to the Eagle Scout award as girls could get back then.  It sounds as though things have changed within the GS organization since I was a member.  
I do think it is important for both boys and girls to have as many enriching life experiences as possible, in whatever agency they choose.

I was surprised to learn about geriatric emergency hospitals for the first time. It was only recently that I discovered Medicare Part B covers medically necessary physician home visits. Just yesterday, late on a Friday afternoon, my mother’s leg veins collapsed, and a painful blister appeared. After speaking with her doctor’s office and consulting family in the medical field, everyone gave the same advice: go to urgent care. Deciding between the ER and urgent care is always difficult and stressful. In this case, it didn’t seem serious enough for the ER, but urgent care still posed significant challenges.

Because I live an hour away, I had to coordinate with relatives who live closer so they could take her to Loma Linda University Urgent Care, which is still a 30-minute drive. My mother is wheelchair-bound, and the temperature was over 100 degrees. Knowing about these services earlier could have spared my parents and our family so much stress and discomfort. I did my research and interviews, and wrote a novel, A Village in the Fields, honoring those Delano Manongs who were brushed aside from the history of the UFW. It came out in 2015, the 50th anniversary of the Delano Grape Strike that started it all. Check out Marissa Aroy’s documentary The Delano Manongs. You’ll learn a lot about these humble heroes. comments.name: PK
comments.body:
Step 1 -- Talk to a bunch of agents, at least 10. Meet them one by one, at the property, and ask a lot of questions -- what could be done to make this house show better and sell for more? What is going on in the neighborhood market today?  How would you market this house (specific details)? What list price or range would you suggest? They will all likely do "comps" which compare your property to other recently sold nearby properties, to determine appropriate price.

Step 2 -- Rank them based on your impressions of their competence, quality of comps, and personal style (especially how well they communicate with you).  Focus on the top 3-4 for the next step, hold the others in reserve for now.

Step 3 -- Tell each of the five they are on your finalist list. Ask them the lowest they will go on agent commission. A fair commission for a sellers agent is 2% to them for selling. And if you want, you can offer to pay some percentage to the buyer's agent. This is traditional but not necessary, as when a buyer submits an offer, it includes what the buyer's  agent wants you to pay, at which point it is negotiable. 

Step 4 -- Choose a winner in your head, but don't inform them yet. First, reach out to all of the ones you didn't choose, thank them and let them know you have chosen someone else. This is only courteous, but also these are agents you may be doing business with again in the future (they are likely to bring you buyers). 

Step 5 -- Inform the winner, get started.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
Again, the biggest tragedy for Taiwan is its geography: too close to mainland China and too far from many of its friends. China's gravity alone can keep Taiwan within its orbit, and that gravitational pull is only growing stronger. Taiwan's options are really limited. 

Working with organizations like FDD strikes me as the wrong footing. Too often, these institutions are filled with keyboard warriors whose analysis can reinforce confrontation rather than reduce it. The fear surrounding the Taiwan Strait is, in my view, amplified by the broader transition to a multipolar world.

I don't think Beijing feels it has to rush unification because the current trajectory largely favors its position. The greater challenge has never been taking Taiwan militarily, but governing it afterward. I think Beijing is clearheaded about that.

Meanwhile, Taiwan's domestic political divisions continue to deepen. At the same time, more Taiwanese continue to travel to mainland China despite repeated warnings from the current administration, and cross-strait travels could even reach a record high this year. From that perspective, why should China not be patient?

comments.name: Christopher Buckley
comments.body: The world is naturally focused on the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, but there's a different kind of contest happening across the Taiwan Strait. China is often deploying "gray zone" methods -- intimidating tactics short of military combat -- to put pressure on Taiwan. Often Taiwanese officials describe these gray zone methods as a bigger worry to them, at least in the nearer term, than invasion. I hope this story explains some of that pressure on Taiwan and how its government is responding.

While there will be numerous , and maybe the majority , of comments blaming the Right for not supporting families like European countries do , you have to ask then why European countries birth rates are also plummeting ? And why are birth rates still relatively high in very poor countries. A big part of the reason is 1) women pursing careers that are high paying , higher education, higher stress and 2) Social media showing younger women partying, traveling , boating , hiking , golfing ,etc. So many women are delaying having kids and focusing on careers and experiences. Nothing wrong at all with either point - but it is a big part if the reason for low fertility rates among ALL developed counties.

This is also part of the reason that in many areas housing prices are so high -its not uncommon in my area of suburban Philly to have a couple in their early 30's buying houses in the $1.5 - $2 million range. It's not every couple of course but you don't need that many high paying career couples chasing limited inventory to push up prices.

comments.body: I’ve noticed that more couples are replacing printed inserts with QR codes, using them to share everything from weekend itineraries to photo galleries and event details. Then came reports that Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce used the technology to help manage guest access at their wedding, and it became clear this wasn’t just a niche trend. QR codes are no longer just for restaurant menus and concert tickets. They’re showing up at weddings, too.

articles.title: QR Codes Make Their Way Down Wedding Aisles
articles.summary: The technology, often associated with pandemic-era menus, is being used by more couples for ease, cost, expedience and sustainability.

comments.name: Brian Michael Coyle
comments.body:
Suppose they peg prices to per capita GDP. Mexico's is around 15,000; Columbia 10,000; Morocco 5,000; Kenya 2,500; Ethiopia 1,000. If a medicine costs 100 in Ethiopia, it's 1,500 in Mexico, the others in-between. 

Now consider the US per capita GDP is around 94,000; Gilead charges 28,000 annually in the US for its daily PrEP. At that rate, in Mexico it would be 5,000, Morocco 1,625, in Ethiopia 330.

If that's how it works, then the issue could be that Gilead starts by charging too much in the US.

A company that charges so much in the US will see providing a medicine below the GDP rate as charity, and pick winners and losers.
